LONDON, Nov 6 : Australian mining billionaire Andrew Forrest said Formula One belonged in a museum and challenged the combustion-engined series to a duel at the launch on Friday of his new all-electric Fortescue Zero Racing Formula E team. The Fortescue founder and executive chairman said he would like to see their respective cars go head-to-head. "I think Formula One has a place," he told reporters. "It should have a very large building with Formula One at the front of it, made out of limestone, with lights on it, and it should be a museum because the younger generation are going to go to the highest performance, greatest technically advanced and kindest to the environment racing there is, and that's going to be Formula E.

"Formula One are fantastic but their time is ticking past them." NEW GEN4 CAR SET TO BE UNLEASHED  Formula E, which has a far smaller global television audience than Formula One, says the new Gen4 car for the 2026/27 season will reach 100kph in about 1.8 seconds and 200kph in 4.2, some 30 per cent faster than a Formula One car. Both series share a common bond through US billionaire John Malone, founder of Formula One owners Liberty Media and Formula E owners Liberty Global. Fortescue Zero Racing is the first Australian-owned Formula E team and was formed after the purchase of Penske Autosport last September. Their Gen4 car will have a powertrain supplied by champions Jaguar with British drivers Dan Ticktum and Taylor Barnard. The company, which acquired Williams Advanced Engineering in 2022 from former Formula One world champions Williams, was involved in Formula E before that as a supplier of battery technology. The Williams connection remains strong, with former marketing head Jim Wright now team principal and Claire Williams, who ran the team founded by her father Frank, an ambassador for Fortescue. The FW initials appear on the new Fortescue car, with Wright and Claire Williams paying tribute also to Australia and Williams' late 1980 F1 world champion Alan Jones, who died on Thursday.  But despite the several Formula One links Forrest, who also described Frank Williams as a mentor, was forthright on that championship. "I want to see Formula One go head to head with Formula E," he declared during the stage presentation. "And then I want to say 'how many decades did they have to get this right, and how many months did we have to get it right'. And let's see how we go. "Let's just put it to the test. I don't care if we come first or second. What I know is that we're doing in months and years what they (Formula One) have taken decades and if we come anywhere near, it's over. "Rise to the challenge, meet the dream. Formula One head-to-head with Formula E. Let's try it on, baby."  The Formula One championship started in 1950 while Formula E's first season was in 2014, when the drivers needed to switch cars mid-race to have enough battery to do a full race distance. Formula One cars now use fully sustainable fuel and the sport last year recorded a 35 per cent reduction in its carbon footprint compared to the 2018 baseline. It says it remains on track to fulfil its commitment to become net-zero carbon by 2030.

Source: Reuters

DUBLIN, Nov 6 : A Hugo Keenan hat-trick helped Ireland find some of the form that has evaded them of late in a 42-12 thrashing of Argentina at the Aviva Stadium as the Nations Championship between the best of the northern and southern hemispheres resumed on Friday. Three more tries from Dan Sheehan, Sam Prendergast and Ronan Kelleher added to the comfortable margin Ireland deserved. Two Mateo Carreras tries, one of which gave Argentina the lead, were all the thoroughly outclassed visitors could muster in response. "The game was never going to be perfect but to win 42-12 first game of the season against a really good side, you have to be really pleased," said coach Andy Farrell, who has challenged his side to turn themselves back into World Cup contenders for next year's tournament. "We can double down hard now on where we can get better, how we can improve and what our new standards are. Be a little bit more ruthless because that's the team that we want to be."

SURPRISE FARRELL SELECTIONS PAY OFF Ireland were the only team among the game's top nations the Pumas had never beaten away and they made the perfect start on 10 minutes when the smallest man on the pitch, Ireland scrumhalf Craig Casey, was no match for Carreras as the winger fielded Tomas Albornoz's pinpoint kick to score in the corner. The hosts struck back with a superb attacking try made and finished by their exciting back three. Rob Baloucoune sped through a gap before finding fellow wing Mack Hansen, who sent fullback Keenan clean through with a brilliant pass inside. Ireland soaked up some pressure before striking off another set piece as Sheehan kept up his remarkable scoring record for a hooker with his 19th try in 42 tests. The hosts grabbed the momentum and never looked back. After struggling badly at the lineout during July's opening tournament games, Ireland's third lineout steal in the space of six minutes resulted in Keenan going over for his second try. The visitors then lost captain Julian Montoya to a head injury and centre Justo Piccardo to a yellow card to limp into halftime 21-5 behind. Farrell had sprung two surprise selections with Casey and flanker Nick Timoney picked ahead of Jamison Gibson-Park and Josh van der Flier. Both rewarded their coach, with Ulster's Timoney in particular adding to a string of strong recent performances. Ireland, who also lost their skipper Sheehan to a head injury, wrapped up the bonus point 71 seconds into the second half as flyhalf Prendergast found a gap in the depleted Argentine ranks to race through for his first international try. Carreras added his second try after Argentina were restored to a full complement but there seemed little chance of avoiding an eighth loss in their last 11 games. Keenan, playing his first home game in an injury-hit 21 months, duly completed his hat-trick on 50 minutes. Hansen, Andrew Porter and Ryan Baird, who said he shed a few tears walking out of the tunnel after a long road back from a leg break, also played very well on their respective returns. Kelleher got on the scoresheet with the easiest of rolling maul tries after Felipe Contepomi's side were again reduced to 14 and the game descended into a ragged final 20 minutes. Ireland began the weekend in fourth place in the tightly contested northern section of the new tournament and face home games against Fiji and South Africa before the finals matches at Twickenham. Argentina next travel to Italy and France.

Source: Reuters

Nov 6 : OpenAI has closed on new funding of $11 billion, the initial part of a round that values the company at $1.25 trillion, a source familiar with the matter said on Friday. The $11 billion raised so far represents only a portion of OpenAI's original target of up to $30 billion, while the company's valuation has come down from the $1.5 trillion level it had initially sought, two investors said. SoftBank and MGX participated in the funding, the investors said. Bloomberg News reported on the funding earlier on Friday. Sentiment toward AI companies has cooled in the last month, with some investors valuing rival Anthropic's planned IPO at about $1.5 trillion, below earlier expectations of roughly $2 trillion.

Source: Reuters

Nov 6 : Audio recording has been disabled on practice courts at the WTA Finals, the governing body's chair said on Friday, after private comments by Jessica Pegula about Mirra Andreeva were broadcast during a livestream this week.  During a practice session at Indian Wells, California, that was streamed on the WTA's YouTube channel, microphones captured a conversation between world number five Pegula and her coach Mark Knowles. The American described French Open champion Andreeva as "a diva" among other remarks that were later circulated on social media, with the WTA taking the blame for failing to inform players about active microphones. WTA chair Valerie Camillo acknowledged there was a lack of signage and notice given to players and said audio will no longer be recorded on practice courts during the tournament, which begins on Sunday.

"The livestream with the audio that was trying to catch ambient sound was active for a period of time, and it's been corrected," WTA chair Valerie Camillo told reporters at Indian Wells. "It's been taken down. There is no more audio recording happening on the practice courts."  Pegula was not asked about the incident during her media availability on Friday but told ESPN that it was an "unfortunate situation" that can hopefully be used to keep pushing for player privacy, which has been an ongoing concern for the WTA this year.  Twice Grand Slam winner Coco Gauff called for more privacy in January after cameras caught her smashing her racket following her Australian Open quarter-final defeat to Elina Svitolina. Several players, including Pegula and six-times Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek, echoed her calls.  "The question is, are we tennis players or are we animals in the zoo, where they are observed even when they poop?" Swiatek said in January. "Okay, that was exaggerating obviously, but it would be nice to have some privacy. It would be nice also to have your own process and not always be observed." Following the incident with Gauff, a WTA tournament in Texas unveiled a "rage room" in February for players to take out their frustrations away from the cameras.  Gauff welcomed the idea of rage rooms but added in April that signage was one of the main solutions. "As a member organization, one of the primary responsibilities of the WTA is to protect our players whenever possible," Camillo said on Friday. "The players deserve better and we will continue to work to raise the bar for the WTA." The season-ending WTA Finals run through November 15.

Source: Reuters

SAO PAULO, Nov 6 : Ferrari held talks to clear the air after a costly clash between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at last weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix, with team principal Frederic Vasseur saying the pair had now moved on and turned their focus to the Sao Paulo race. The meeting followed Hamilton’s public criticism of the opening-lap incident, which derailed Ferrari's hopes of a one-two finish, with the Briton saying again on Thursday that he remained frustrated by what had happened. "We did it yesterday evening," Vasseur told reporters at Interlagos on Friday. "It was good to discuss, good to clarify my position and their position. It was good to do, and now we turn the page and we are focusing on the next one." Leclerc, who became a father this week, arrived in Brazil on Thursday but missed the first practice session, with youngster Dino Beganovic standing in for the Monegasque.

Hamilton started from pole in Mexico but lost out after a battle with Leclerc through the opening corners forced both Ferraris off track, allowing race winner Max Verstappen to take advantage. The seven-times world champion said after the race that it was difficult when a "teammate works against you" and suggested Ferrari needed to revisit how their drivers raced one another. Vasseur said the team's expectations had not changed despite the flare-up. "The guidelines are still the same," he said. "They need to respect each other. They are two competitors with the fighting spirit for sure, but they need to have respect for the other one. But mainly, they need to respect the brand, the team." Vasseur also dismissed suggestions that differences in personality between Hamilton and Leclerc posed a broader problem for the Maranello-based team. "We have two experienced guys, two competitive guys... It's a choice in the lineup. I have the positive and the negative. I will deal with the negative. "I'm not asking them to be best friends. I think it's even probably a bit negative. I'm just asking them to act and to work as professionals," he added. The situation prompted a familiar reaction from Mercedes boss Toto Wolff, who likened the episode to the intense rivalry between Hamilton and Nico Rosberg during Mercedes' title-dominating years in the 2010s. "Fred here doesn't need any advice from me, but it's like a deja vu," Wolff said. "Sometimes it needs the really tough ones, like the last one, to make a point."

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 6 : Wall Street equities mostly rallied on Friday, reversing course after trillions of dollars of world stock market value were wiped out over fears that Democratic election victories this week would bring tighter US regulations for the AI industry. The benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq finished higher, with technology, communication services and industrials stocks driving gains. The Dow ended lower. All three indexes notched weekly losses following a brutal selloff in the prior session. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.46 per cent, the S&P 500 rose 0.31 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.1 per cent. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was up 4.2 per cent after slumping in its biggest one-day drop since April 2025. Nvidia rose nearly 3 per cent, after its worst day since January 2025, when the emergence of low-cost Chinese AI model DeepSeek hammered markets.

Other heavyweight chipmakers, including AMD, Intel, and Micron Technology, closed up between 5 per cent and 11 per cent, while Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were also up 4 per cent and nearly 9 per cent respectively after losses earlier this week. "Most of the disruption of the AI buildout will not probably occur but it's just the uncertainty of the change in government from Republican-led to Democratic-led, not only at the federal level but the state, local levels," said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management. "That's causing some disruption in the expectations of investors ... The volatility around elections or any political event, whether it be war or terrorist attack, is always going to disrupt the market." Texas' Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state — which already has a large share of US data centres — will introduce new laws to protect local communities from their further mass buildup. The jitters are hitting an AI trade already under pressure from fears that the massive cost of the data centres and other infrastructure will limit future returns, spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike. RIPPLE EFFECT The bounces were in stark contrast with market action in the rest of the world. Europe's STOXX 600 lost 1 per cent. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's KOSPI both slumped about 6 per cent. For the Nikkei — just like Wall Street the previous day — it was the biggest one-day drop since US President Donald Trump's "Liberation Day" trade tariff panic of April 2025. The MSCI All-World index fell 0.68 per cent while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost nearly 3 per cent. PAYROLLS BEAT FORECASTS US nonfarm payrolls, usually one of the most-watched pieces of data, but largely overshadowed by the tech drama, showed a stronger-than-expected 165,000 pickup in jobs. An anticipated slowdown in annual wage growth to below 3 per cent for the first time in nearly 5-1/2 years did not materialise either, as it came in at 3.1 per cent. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note ticked up to 4.86 per cent, having dropped to its lowest level since September 9 overnight. In currencies, the dollar rose against major currencies including the euro, yen and Swiss franc. It was up 0.52 per cent against the yen and rose 0.47 per cent against the Swiss franc. The euro was down 0.68 per cent against the dollar at $1.1142. Brent crude prices settled at $98.32, rising just 0.03 per cent, on hopes the midterms' results might prompt Trump to de-escalate the Iran war. Spot gold was flat at $4,066.28 per ounce.

CHICAGO, Nov 6 : The US Department of Agriculture will use an artificial intelligence tool it built to check data in next week's monthly crop production report, agency officials said, after a series of data missteps eroded farmers' and traders' trust in its forecasts. After the USDA discovered errors in its corn data from September, officials determined the AI tool would have flagged the problem and decided to use it on the crop production report due on November 10, USDA Under Secretary Scott Hutchins said in an interview. The tool's debut tests whether the agency can restore confidence in data that often moves markets.  "I'm very bullish on the fact that we'll be able to utilize these tools in the future to help us avoid these kinds of really, truly unfortunate errors," Hutchins said on Thursday.

Last month, the USDA corrected its September corn production and yield data. The correction raised the yield estimate by about 3 per cent in Nebraska, the third-biggest corn-producing state, and lowered it by about 2 per cent in Kansas.  The agency, long viewed as the gold standard of global agricultural market information, previously faced criticism after it made sharp upward revisions to estimates for last year's corn acreage. Over the summer, it  reported inaccurate beef export sales data. The USDA previously said it was launching a pilot project that would rely more heavily on technology to improve crop acreage and yield estimates as fewer farmers respond to its surveys.  COMPUTER FILE ERROR  Lance Honig, chair of the agricultural statistics board for USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service, told Reuters that a computer file incorrectly combined data on irrigated and non-irrigated corn acres gathered by field surveyors, causing the errors in September's data. Kansas and Nebraska were affected because they have higher percentages of irrigated fields, which often have higher yields, he said.  "This error that occurred in September is literally a very isolated occurrence that, quite frankly, with the proper validation, we should have caught," Honig said. "There was no issue with the data that was gathered at the field level." The errors angered farmers who are struggling to make money as they pay soaring prices for diesel, fertilizer and other inputs. Last month, the National Corn Growers Association, which represents 35,000 farmers, said the September errors were unacceptable and had further hurt farmers' confidence in the USDA's ability to produce accurate reports. "You just don't know what the USDA is going to do anymore," said Jim Gerlach, president of brokerage A/C Trading in Indiana, on Friday. "Their reports have become so erratic." Questions around the credibility of federal data increased after President Donald Trump's administration sharply downsized the government last year. Thousands of employees at the USDA have left, and experts have worried the cuts hobbled the agency's ability to produce accurate and timely data. Hutchins said the September errors were not related to staffing losses. The new AI tool will add to, not replace, the agency's data validation, he said.  "The tool is basically going to be used as a check to make sure that there are no anomalies that we were not able to see or identify in the normal process," Hutchins said.       This week, market analysts questioned the accuracy of another monthly USDA report on soy processing which showed a sharp divide between how many soybeans were crushed and how much soymeal was produced in Iowa.  The USDA said it was reviewing the report as part of a normal process and would make any necessary revisions next month.

Source: Reuters
